entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Yin Mo (courtesy name Siqian) was a pivotal Confucian scholar, astrologer, and high-ranking official who served the state of Shu Han during the tumultuous Three Kingdoms period of China (220–280 CE). His intellectual contributions spanned astronomy, classical exegesis, and legal administration, making him a central figure in the intellectual and governmental fabric of Shu Han, particularly under Emperor Liu Bei and his successor Liu Shan. Born in Zitong Commandery (modern Mianyang, Sichuan province), Yin Mo's expertise was crucial in legitimizing and stabilizing the nascent Shu Han regime through his mastery of traditional Chinese scholarship and his practical administrative skills, which were highly valued in an era of political fragmentation and intense military competition. He represents the ideal of the scholar-official whose intellectual depth directly informed statecraft during a foundational period of Chinese history.

Initially avoiding official service during the chaos preceding the Three Kingdoms, Yin Mo was eventually recruited by Liu Bei, the founding emperor of Shu Han, around 214 CE, following Liu Bei's capture of Yi Province. He rose steadily through the ranks, holding various significant positions including Grand Administrator of Guanghan (廣漢太守), Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat (尚書令), and ultimately the prestigious role of Grand Tutor (太傅) to the crown prince Liu Shan. His administrative work involved drafting legal codes and advising on state policy, while his scholarly endeavors focused on the rigorous study of the Classics, particularly the *Book of Documents* and the *Zuo Zhuan*, and the refinement of astronomical calculations. Yin Mo was renowned for his profound understanding of ancient texts and his ability to interpret omens and celestial phenomena, which were considered vital for imperial legitimacy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Yin Mo's contributions as a scholar and high-ranking official were crucial for the administrative stability and ideological legitimacy of the Shu Han state, influencing its governance and the education of its second emperor, Liu Shan. His work helped preserve classical learning during a period of intense political upheaval.
